sections.report:
**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Do the main image and the headline make one idea together, with neither just repeating the other?** No. The figure (about x 96–656, y 220–420) is a flat drawing of grey and blue blocks: a pale rectangle, a dark slab, a light-blue band and a blue rounded bar. The headline, the copy and the caption ("The new north landing, seen from the water at low tide") are about wider ramps, a covered waiting area, benches, a kiosk and ramps that meet the deck at every tide. The picture shows none of these, so it cannot back up the page's main claim. That claim is that prams and wheelchairs now roll straight on. The reader gets a box that looks like a wireframe placeholder. They can't see the new landing, and the caption describes a view that isn't there. There's a second problem: the blue rounded bar (about x 496–606, y 340–364) has the same blue and the same corner radius as the **Sign up** button (x 789–888, y 293–337). In a page with a form, it looks like a control. Fix: show the actual rebuilt landing, ideally a photo or a drawing where the level ramp meets the deck, so the picture proves the headline's claim. Keep the button blue out of any non-interactive drawing. Defect. Common sense: the catalogue entry "Visual and headline work together" has no approved source. **Major**, because this is the only picture and the page exists to show the rebuild.
2. **Is the copy finished, with no placeholder text and no spelling mistakes?** No. The footer line at about y 750 ("Ferry timetables are a sample for a fixture image. All names and places are invented.") is test or fixture copy, not text for passengers. With the block-shape figure, it makes the page read as unfinished. There are no spelling mistakes. Fix: replace it with real footer content, such as the operator's name, contact details and the date of the update, or remove it. If this is deliberately a test fixture, it isn't a finding. Defect for a published page. Common sense, since the catalogue has no entry for this. **Minor.**

**What's working.**
- The second paragraph ("The ramps now meet the deck at every tide, so prams and wheelchairs roll straight on.") ends on what the change means for the reader, not just what was built. That's the strongest line on the page, and it should lead.
- The page holds one calm, civic mood throughout. There is one sans-serif family, a muted blue-grey palette with a single saturated blue, and flat horizontals with square, lightly rounded shapes. That suits a transport notice and reads as one piece, not a collage.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 6 yes, 2 no (main image and headline make one idea; copy finished, no placeholder).

sections.report:
**First read.** The eye goes first to "Landing stage rebuild" at top left. It then crosses to the bold "Get timetable changes" heading and the blue "Sign up" button, and comes back to the illustration. The page reads as a short ferry-service news page with a sign-up card beside it. It feels calm and orderly.

**Assumed job.** A local ferry operator's web page telling passengers about the rebuilt landing and inviting them to sign up for timetable notices.

**Walk: What matters first**
- Does one element stand clearly above the rest? **Yes.** The title is about 32 px bold, the largest and darkest thing on the page. The card heading (about 22 px) and the blue button are clearly secondary.
- Can you tell each text level from the next, with no two sizes almost the same? **Yes.** I count about four levels: title about 32, card heading about 22, body about 18, and labels, caption and footnote all about 13. The gaps between them are clear.
- Do headings that are larger than the text also differ in weight, form, or color? **Yes.** Both the title and the card heading are bold, and the body is regular.

Every line is yes, so there are no entries to open. (I could not run Bash in this session. The image is about one screen, so I worked from the whole image.)

**Section.** What matters first: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **One clear starting point.** The title at about 32 px bold (96,58 to 455,95) is the only element that size and weight. It sits top left, where a left-to-right reader starts anyway. The eye lands there without competition, even with the blue button and the blue boat shape nearby.
- **Few sizes with big gaps between them.** The page uses roughly four sizes and makes finer distinctions with weight instead of more sizes. For example, "Get timetable changes" is set apart from the 18 px body by bold weight as well as size. So the card heading reads as a heading for its own area, below the page title and above the body, with nothing in between that looks like an accident.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 3 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

I've checked the alignment and spacing and read the reference entries. Now I'm writing the arrangement report.

**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Do all blocks, pictures included, take their edges and the gaps between them from one grid, so column lines and gutters repeat down the page?** No.
   - **Where:** The figure (x 96–656, y 220–420) sits in a text column whose lines run out to about x 686–696.
   - **What the viewer sees:** The picture stops about 30–40 px short of the column it sits in. Its right edge doesn't match the text measure, the panel, or any other line on the page. It's too close to the column edge to look like a deliberate inset, so it reads as a near-miss (Arnheim, *Art and Visual Perception*, ch. I: an ambiguous placement makes the eye waver and the page look unfinished).
   - **Why:** Müller-Brockmann, *Grid Systems in Graphic Design* ("The photograph in the grid system") says a picture takes its width from the columns.
   - **Fix:** Make the figure the full width of the text column, or narrow the text measure to the figure's width, so the two share a right edge.
   - Convention. Weight: minor.
2. **Does the visual weight balance, with no side, crowded or empty, that makes the page look about to tip?** No.
   - **Where:**
     - The two columns together span x 96–1120, leaving a 96 px left margin against 160 px on the right.
     - Everything with weight (headline, figure, the blue button, the bordered panel) sits above y 530.
     - Below that there is only the one-line footnote at y 750.
   - **What the viewer sees:** The content block looks pushed up and to the left in the window. The bottom 40% of the frame and the lower right (under the panel, x 760–1120, y 420–800) carry nothing. The page reads as unfinished, or as if content failed to load, rather than as calm (Arnheim, *Art and Visual Perception*, ch. I "Balance": a heavy side needs a counterweight).
   - **Fix:**
     - Make the outer margins equal, or centre the 1024 px content block in the frame.
     - Either let the footnote follow the content rather than sit at the viewport floor, or give the lower area a purpose.
     - If this is a viewport capture of a short page, the first two changes are enough.
   - Convention. Weight: minor.

**What's working.**
- The left column's spacing groups cleanly. The headline sits close to its paragraph, the caption is tight under the figure (about 16 px), and the gaps before the figure and before the next paragraph are larger, so each group reads at a glance.
- The sign-up panel holds exactly one group: heading, two fields, button, and the reassurance note. A clear gutter of about 75 px separates it from the article, so the article and the form never read as one unit.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 11 yes, 2 no (one grid governs the page, pictures included; weight balances).

**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- The body measure suits a reading page. The first paragraph (x≈96–683, y≈122–196) runs about 66 characters per line. Its line spacing is comfortable for that width, and it is set flush left in a plain sans with a soft, even rag. It reads at a single steady pace, as Bringhurst's 45 to 75 character range intends.
- The text uses one family with clear steps between sizes: the 34 px bold heading, the ~18 px body, the ~20 px bold form heading and the ~12–13 px caption, labels, helper note and footer. Each size has an obvious job. All the text is near-black on white, so nothing reads as faint, not even the small helper note under "Sign up" (y≈362–382).

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 30 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure.

**Section.** Color: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Is strong, saturated color kept to a small share of the area, with most of the area neutral or muted?** The share of strong color is small, but it fails the accent-restraint part of this line. The page's one saturated color is the blue of the "Sign up" button (about x 789–888, y 293–337). The same blue also fills the boat in Figure 1 (about x 496–606, y 340–364), which is a rounded rectangle about the size of a button. That blue boat is the most saturated thing in the left column and the only strong colour on the page outside the button, so the eye gets pulled into a decorative illustration. Its shape and colour also make it look clickable, so a viewer may try to click it. And because the colour no longer belongs only to the action, "Sign up" stops being the one blue thing on the page. The source is Apple HIG, Color, and Material Design 3, Color roles: keep one accent for the main action and interactive states, and don't use it to decorate content that isn't interactive. Fix: keep the accent blue for "Sign up" (and links, if there are any). Draw the boat in a muted or neutral tone from the illustration's own slate range, such as a darker slate blue or a warm off-hue that isn't the accent, so it still reads as the subject without looking like a control. Convention. Weight: minor. The form is still easy to find in its bordered card on the right, so this weakens the button's emphasis and adds a small false cue but doesn't hide the action.

**What's working.** The palette is tight: a cool neutral range (white page, near-black text, pale grey-blue sky, slate pier, muted blue water) plus one accent. Nothing competes on hue, and the page feels calm and of a piece. The lightness range is clear too. The dark slate deck stands out against the pale sky and mid-blue water, and the text is near-black on white, so the figure and the page structure would both still read in grayscale.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 8 yes, 1 no (strong color kept to a small share: the accent blue is reused on the boat illustration)

sections.report:
**Section.** Pictures: applies. There is one figure, the illustration at 96–656 × 220–420 px.

**Findings**
1. **Does every image show its content, with no broken-image icon or empty placeholder box?** No. Figure 1 is made of flat boxes: a pale sky, a dark grey slab (156–456, 330–360), a lighter grey box (176–296, 280–330), a blue rounded bar (496–606, 340–364) and a light blue water band. The caption promises "the new north landing, seen from the water at low tide". The text around it talks about wider ramps, a covered waiting area, benches facing the water, a kiosk, and ramps that meet the deck at every tide. The picture shows none of these. A reader looks to it for proof that prams and wheelchairs can roll straight on and gets a wireframe. It reads as a stand-in that was never replaced. That makes the caption feel untrue and makes the article look unfinished. Also, the blue bar is the same blue and corner shape as the "Sign up" button 150 px to its right, so it looks more like a stray button than a boat. This check has no catalog entry, so it rests on common sense. If a real photo or illustration is meant to load here, this finding falls away. Fix: use a photo or a drawn illustration that clearly shows the ramp meeting the deck at low tide, plus the covered area and benches. At minimum, draw the ramp. Give the boat its own colour and shape so it doesn't echo the interface button. Defect. Weight: major.
2. **Does each crop look intended, with no limb cut at a joint and no edges that just touch?** No. The bottom edge of the dark slab sits exactly on the waterline at y≈360. Because the two edges just touch, you can't tell whether the deck floats, stands on piles, or is cut off by the water. At low tide the deck should stand clearly above the water, so this muddies the one thing the caption names. Fix: lift the deck clear of the water and show its supports and the ramp angle, or sink it in on purpose. Either way, don't let the two edges coincide. The catalog entry's source is off the approved list, so this rests on common sense. Defect (small). Weight: minor.
3. **Does the subject of each picture stand clearly apart from its background?** No. The light grey box (176–296, 280–330), presumably the covered waiting area, is a pale grey on a pale blue-grey sky and nearly vanishes. Yet the text names it as one of the two headline improvements. Fix: give the shelter a clearly darker or more saturated value than the sky so it reads as an object. The catalog entry's source is off the approved list, so this rests on common sense. Defect (small). Weight: minor.

**What's working.** The figure is crisp flat vector art with no stretching or compression, so it's ready to take a proper drawing at this size. The caption is numbered, sits right under the figure, and says where the view is taken from and when, which is exactly what a caption should do once the picture matches it.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** Whether the figure is a final illustration or a placeholder for a photo that failed to load. Check the live page and the source asset. If a real image should be there, finding 1 is a loading bug, not a design choice.

**Checklist.** Pictures: 12 lines, 9 yes, 3 no (every image shows its content; crops look intended, no touching edges; subject stands apart from its background)

I couldn't run `scripts/entries.mjs` because Bash was denied, so I read `references/art-direction.md` directly. That confirmed the figure-ground entry's source is off the approved list. I didn't reach the entry for cropping and framing, so finding 2 is judged on common sense.

sections.report:
**Section.** Charts and data: skipped. The page has no chart, no table of figures, no dashboard and no headline number. Figure 1 is a flat illustration of the landing, not a data display.

**Findings**
None.

**Checklist.** Charts and data: skipped

**Section.** Interface: applies. There is a two-field sign-up form with one button in the right-hand card.

**Findings**
1. **Is everything the user needs to act visible on this screen, with nothing to remember from another?** The form card is at about x 760–1120, y 56–420. It asks only for "Your name" and "Home landing". The note under the button (y 355–390) says "We send one short note when the timetable changes", but nothing on the form says where the note goes. There is no email field, no phone field, and no sign of an account the person is already logged into. A reader who wants the alerts can't tell how they will reach them, so they may not trust it, or they may sign up and never hear anything. On the other hand, the form asks for a name, which the service doesn't need in order to send a timetable alert. **Defect.** This is common sense; no catalog entry was opened, because Bash was refused, so the entries script couldn't run. The fix is to add the one contact field the service needs (email, or a phone number for texts) and say which one in the note ("We email you once when…"). Drop or make optional the name field unless it is used. If the user is already signed in, show where the note will go ("Sent to b…@…"). **Weight: major.** As shown, the form can't do its one job.
2. **Do the inputs allow only valid values, by pickers, input types, or disabled options?** "Home landing" (x 789–1091, y 237–277) is a blank text box. The landings are a fixed, known set, so a free text box invites misspellings, nicknames and "north" vs "North landing". Those won't match a route, and the reader won't get the alerts they asked for. It also makes them recall the exact name of their landing instead of picking it from a list. **Defect / convention** (Nielsen 5, Error prevention; Norman, Constraints). The fix is a select menu, or radio buttons if there are only a few landings. It could also default to the landing this article is about. **Weight: major.** It is the field that decides which alerts the reader gets.
3. **Does every control look like what it does, buttons pressable, fields typeable, and links marked by more than color?** The boat in the illustration (about x 496–606, y 340–364) is a rounded rectangle in exactly the same blue as the "Sign up" button (x 789–888, y 293–337). On a page where that blue means "press this", it reads for a moment as a second button. Some people will try to click it. **Taste/common sense**: it is a false signifier, the reverse of Norman's signifiers. The fix is to keep the action blue for actions only and draw the boat in a different color, or give it a hull shape. **Weight: minor.**
4. **Are required or optional fields marked?** Neither field is marked. With two fields, people will mostly guess right, but if name turns out to be optional (see finding 1), nothing tells them. **Convention** (forms: required markers). The fix is to mark the optional field "(optional)", or remove it. **Weight: minor.**
5. **Do the navigation and components follow the conventions users know from the platform and similar products?** The page has no header, no site name or logo, and no navigation. Nothing links to the timetables themselves, even though the form is about timetable changes. A reader who arrives from a link can't tell whose service this is or get to the timetable. That also weakens trust in a form asking for personal details. **Convention** (Jakob's law). This may be a cropped page or a single component, and if the real page has a site header, this finding doesn't apply. Otherwise the fix is a standard header with the operator's name and a link to the timetables. **Weight: minor.**

**What's working.**
- There is exactly one primary action. "Sign up" is the only filled, solid-blue control, it is clearly pressable, and it looks about 99×44 px, so the target is easily large enough.
- The fields themselves are done right. Each has a visible label above it, sitting closer to its own box than to the field above. The input borders are a dark grey-blue that looks well over 3:1 against the white. The note under the button gives short help exactly where the commitment is made, and it promises "you can stop the notes at any time".

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- Focus indicator on the two fields and the button: check it is at least 2 px thick and has 3:1 contrast.
- What the form does on an empty or invalid submit: errors named in words, next to the field.

**Checklist.** Interface: 33 lines, 27 yes, 5 no (nothing to remember from another screen, since there is no contact field; inputs allow only valid values; controls look like what they do; required or optional marked; platform conventions), 1 unsure (focus indicator).

I couldn't open the catalog entries because Bash was refused, so the findings rest on the checklist lines and the critic's guidance only, without the entries' "How bad it gets" detail.
